summary.short: Enacts Utah Code 13-72a and 58-60-118 regulating mental health chatbots that use generative AI. Suppliers may not sell or share Utah users' health information or chat input, must restrict and disclose advertising and disclose AI status, and may file a policy for an affirmative defense. Takes effect May 7, 2025.
summary.long: H.B. 452 amends Utah Code 13-2-1 to add a new Chapter 72a to the chapters administered by the Division of Consumer Protection, and enacts Chapter 72a and 58-60-118. It defines mental health chatbot, generative artificial intelligence and Utah user, the last by location in the state. Suppliers may not sell or share individually identifiable health information or user input of a Utah user with third parties, subject to exceptions for disclosures to a health care provider with consent, to a health plan on request, and to associated third parties under HIPAA-referenced security provisions. A supplier may not use a mental health chatbot to advertise unless the advertisement is clearly identified and sponsorships and affiliations are disclosed, and may not use user input to select or customize advertising, except for advertising the chatbot itself. The chatbot must disclose that it is artificial intelligence and not a human before access, at the start of an interaction after seven days of non-use, and when asked. The Division of Consumer Protection enforces the chapter, with administrative fines of up to $2,500 per violation; courts may grant injunctions, disgorgement and fines of up to $2,500 per violation, and impose civil penalties of up to $5,000 for violating an order. Under 58-60-118, a supplier has an affirmative defense to liability under 58-1-501 if it created, maintained and implemented a written policy covering listed matters such as therapist involvement, testing, harm reporting and risk response, keeps related documentation, files the policy with the division for a fee, and complies with it. The defense does not bar division actions and does not recognize a chatbot as a therapist. The chapter contains a severability clause. The bill takes effect May 7, 2025.

notes: Relations and entities are drawn only from the enrolled bill text; target_instrument_id is left empty because no registry IDs were assigned. Several cross-referenced provisions (13-72-101, 13-11-3, 58-1-501, 63A-19-101, 63J-1-504, 13-2-8, 58-60-102, 45 C.F.R. Parts 160 and 164) are not reproduced in this document, so their content is not verified here. 58-60-118 creates a defense that applies only to actions under 58-1-501(1) or (2), which the text does not set out. The bill's 13-2-1(2) uses brackets to mark deleted list items, including the Social Media Regulation Act chapter. Section 13-72a-101(5) lacks an opening quotation mark before the defined term 'Division'. The fine of up to $2,500 per violation appears in both 13-72a-204(3)(a) and (4)(e), which is consistent. section_status entries are marked not_applicable only because the schema requires that field; both sections have entries above.
